title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
description: Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and
body: Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing."And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction. "The result was that the state grew by stealth."The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no. "Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."As their conference gets under way in Birmingham the Conservatives have pledged to end a childcare "cliff edge", which currently means parents earning more than £100,000 do not qualify for the entitlement.The party has also promised to deliver 50,000 new prison places by slashing the overseas aid budget to £1bn a year in a bid to end the early release of offenders.Over the 14 years the Conservatives were in power, around 500 net prison places were created, which takes into account 14,142 added in existing and new jails, set against 13,660 lost mainly to dilapidation and closures.Speaking in the main conference hall, Badenoch sought to make the case that the party had moved on from 2024 and outlined her expectation that the next few days in Birmingham would be a chance for members to discuss their ideas.She said: "We're going to be having debates, we're going to have arguments, they are going to be fun."We're going to challenge each other and afterwards we're still going to be a united party."During a question and answer session, Badenoch focused on different topics covered in her essay – including citizenship and how communities need to operate on trust.She said the UK is "not a dormitory, it is not a hotel" before speaking how "British culture means something".To applause in the well-attended hall, Badenoch said: "I don't want lots of little ghettos of separatist communities where they are recreating the place they come from - that will ruin the United Kingdom."Responding, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the Tory Party "is stuck in the past and remains completely out of touch with what people across Britain want to see"."Last week Andy Burnham set out a plan to bring back hope to Britain. Kemi Badenoch wants to drag our country back to a politics that let so many people down over the past 40 years."

schema.headline: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch

title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
description: The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.The measu
body: The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption. One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition. Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day. Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when further tickets go on sale in October and January. Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free. The exhibition opened on 10 September but has experienced a series of problems with queues and congestion, with some visitors spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry.Visitors were later stopped from taking photographs and a recorded message was introduced encouraging people to continue moving through the one-way exhibition.The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain.Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses.The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027.The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago.

schema.headline: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues

title: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory
description: Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government.S
body: Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government.Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil.On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east."Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.

schema.headline: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory

title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion
description: Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party.The pa
body: Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party.The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".Activists endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of members at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1022 votes to 813.Discussion about the vote has dominated the conference, and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last election. The motion adopted by Green members defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine"."The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says. It has attracted criticism from some Jewish groups, including the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council who wrote a letter to the party ahead of the vote.In a statement on Sunday evening, the organisations called the motion an "attack on the Jewish community"."Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it," it said."Branding most British Jews and Jewish institutions 'racist' stokes anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed."Israel's Foreign Ministry said the motion went beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate" and was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom".Later on Sunday, it said Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar had banned Polanski from entering Israel in response.Debate about the motion, as well as the conflict in Gaza, has featured heavily during the conference, which is taking place after a surge in its membership in the wake of Polanski's election as leader in September last year. Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression"."We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added. Polanski himself did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here. Asked about the motion on Friday, Polanski said: "If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party."However, he said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."He had also said he wanted to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.However, both amendments favoured by Polanski were rejected by Green members.The Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council statement referred to a "particular criticism" for Polanski "who neither spoke against the motion nor voted" but welcomed the subsequent "cross-party condemnation".A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.Speaking after the motion had been approved, chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein told the BBC she could consider her future in the party. Polanski has not specified whether he supports the motion passed by members, but added his name to a joint statement from the party's five MPs and deputy leaders issued after the vote.The statement pledged to ensure the Green Party was "an anti-racist party in every way" and added that there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people".Over the course of the three-day conference, key figures in the party have expressed differing positions about the Zionism motion. Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, with Denyer arguing it could risk "alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people".Chowns, as well as former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas, both spoke against the motion during the debate.Addressing members, Lucas said: "I urge you not to support the over-simplification at the heart of this motion - a refusal to accept complexities which is leading to so many Jewish members feeling scared and unwelcome in our party."Deputy leader Mothin Ali, who had expressed support for the motion before the vote, said it was calling for "a state that's democratic, that guarantees the rights of every single person living on that land".He added that he was "absolutely not" calling all Jewish people who define themselves as Zionists racist.Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election. The Conservatives criticised the motion, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core". Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards"."It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she added.Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK.He added: "This is a divisive motion that pours fuel on the fire of tensions in the UK, and will leave many British Jews feeling less safe."

schema.headline: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion

title: Andrew Griffith to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations
description: Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building c
body: Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building costs.Griffith and his colleagues will use day two of the party's conference in Birmingham to also explain how they would want to reduce food costs, support Heathrow Airport expansion and abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency. Another prospective policy is replacing agreements designed to compel developers to fund community projects and services in areas they want to build.Griffith will describe his approach as the "most ambitious deregulation project in a generation". Reform UK suggested the Tories were "copying our policies".Griffith's speech comes after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch published a 100-page document, external explaining her guiding principles and how her party would act should it return to government by winning the next general election.Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government, including on the economy, between 2010 and 2024. Griffith is expected to say: "No-one else is coming to save our economy.  Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation."He will accuse Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to pursue a "socialist fever dream of the 1970s", adding the Tories want to deliver "cheaper homes, lower taxes, and less red tape".Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".During a series of speeches on Monday, Conservative shadow ministers will continue to make their case and provide more details of their proposals.This will include ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, including the future homes standard. The Tories believe their changes could cut the cost of delivering a new home by up to £50,000, which in turn they expect could save money for buyers.A single levy for developers would be implemented in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.The Conservatives argue this new charge would remove delays and improve how the funds are spent to the benefit of residents.The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would also be scrapped by the Conservatives.The party believes this would help lift a "burden" from businesses and in turn could cut the cost of the weekly shop.On Heathrow, Griffith is expected to say the next Conservative government would do "whatever it takes to end the delays and boost capacity by backing the third runway".Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves championed the runway to boost the economy after Labour won power, although Burnham has refused to say whether he backs the project since becoming prime minister.Burnham has described it as "principally... a matter for London and Londoners".Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies". He added the Tories were unable to match Reform's pledge to raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

schema.headline: Andrew Griffith to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations

title: WRC: Elfyn Evans becomes world champion after late Oliver Solberg crash
description: Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC championImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin won just two of 13 r
body: Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC championImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin won just two of 13 races in the 2026 WRC seasonElfyn Evans became Britain's first world rally champion for 25 years after rival Oliver Solberg crashed in a highly dramatic finish to the season in Italy.Sweden's Solberg was on course to snatch the lead on the final stage of the last round of the World Rally Championship, and thereby deny Evans the title.But Solberg lost control of his car with a few hundred metres to go in the Rally Italia Sardegna, which meant the glory went to Welshman Evans, a five-time runner-up in the championship."It hasn't sunk in," said a shocked Evans."I was sure it was over. I feel for Oliver - he had an incredible weekend. I don't know what to say."The 37-year-old and co-driver Scott Martin had led for much of the 2026 season and took a 21-point advantage into the final round in Sardinia.But that gap had shrunk to a solitary point by the time the drivers lined up for the last of 17 stages, bringing back painful memories of previous narrow misses for Evans.Solberg, 25, needed only to beat his Toyota team-mate in the final stage to claim enough bonuses to be champion, but he crashed two corners from the finish.Evans becomes only the third British man to win the WRC title after Colin McRae in 1995 and Richard Burns in 2001.Figure caption, World champion Evans reflects on 'incredible finish'Solberg, whose father Petter won the WRC title in 2003, won the rally by almost a minute ahead of nine-time world champion Sebastien Ogier.With barely a kilometre to run of the final stage he and English co-driver Elliott Edmondson were 1.9 seconds up on Evans and closing at speed on the championship.Though Solberg got back on the road, his crash meant he finished nine seconds slower than his team-mate - and five points behind Evans in the overall standings.A third Toyota driver, Sami Pajari, finished a further one point behind in third - having seen his own title challenge evaporate on the final weekend.An inconsolable Solberg remained in his car for some time at the end of the stage before being encouraged to take to the podium by Gazoo Racing team principal Jari-Matti Latvala and team-mate Ogier."Two corners, two corners," said an emotional Solberg."First congratulations to Elfyn, he has been very consistent all season. That I even had a shot after my rollercoaster of a season is incredible."I tried everything. I knew I was pushing but didn't know if it was enough. I pushed even more and I couldn't save the car. I tried my very best."Evans, from Dolgellau in north Wales, had previously missed out on the title on the final day three times and in two of those seasons he had taken a lead into the concluding rally before losing out to Ogier in 2020 and 2025."I don't really know what my reaction is. It's surreal with how it happened. It's a relief," he said."It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done."For Toyota sporting director Kaj Lindstrom there were mixed feelings."That was the hardest thing. The ending was quite something, I didn't expect it," said the Finn."It was a good fight and we all saw that Oliver was all or nothing. It held all the way to the end."Oliver still has time but Elfyn finally got his title so we're really happy for him."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jon Armstrong was competing in his first full season at the top level in the World Rally ChampionshipThe WRC season was reduced to 13 rounds when the Saudi Arabia event, originally planned for next month, was cancelled because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.Rally Italia Sardegna marked the end of Jon Armstrong's rookie season at the top level of WRC, and he produced his best result when finishing seventh."It's been good to have a clean weekend with a strong result," said the M-Sport Ford driver."It's not been an easy year and this was a rally to show we can put it together. A big thanks to everyone who has been supporting us, it's been a great year and it's been a privilege to drive this car."Armstrong's team-mate and fellow Irishman Josh McErlean did not fare as well despite running as high as sixth on Saturday before retiring after a collision with a tree.He also had to stop twice on Sunday before finishing well off the pace but claimed ninth spot in the championship.Rally Italia Sardegna result1. title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
description: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to
body: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel. Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

schema.headline: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country

title: NFL London: 'Money-grab' or celebration? London series begins amid anger over ticket prices
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Neither the Washington Commanders nor Indianapolis Colts qualified for last season's play-offsByBen CollinsBB
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Neither the Washington Commanders nor Indianapolis Colts qualified for last season's play-offsByBen CollinsBBC Sport journalist at Tottenham Hotspur StadiumOnce upon a time, tickets for NFL games in London were like gold dust.All 43 games have been near capacity at Wembley, Twickenham and Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.According to the NFL, its UK fanbase has swelled to 18.6 million, with 4.5 million of those considered 'avid' fans.So in the build-up to this year's London series, why were thousands of tickets still available for two of the three games?Next week's clash between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham sold out in hours.But the crowd for Sunday's game at Tottenham between Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts only reached 60,907 after ticket prices were slashed, and large sections remain unsold for the Wembley game on 18 October.The NFL is playing a record nine regular-season games abroad this season but 19 years after the first London game, has the NFL reached a saturation point in the UK?Why have ticket sales been slow?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Most of the fans BBC Sport spoke to at Sunday's game had travelled from the United StatesTickets to see Indianapolis beat Washington 30-13 on Sunday went on sale in July at £79-£245.But the NFL then dropped prices twice, in late August and again last week. That meant some fans who paid £185 were sat next to fans who paid £79 a few days ago.Some tickets were also discounted or free via the Blue Light Card and Tickets For Good platforms.Matt Cullen has travelled from Cambridge to most of the London games and said there were two main reasons for the slow sales; a price hike and a season-ticket package being scrapped."I find the prices now mind-boggling," he added. "It's so far above the rate of inflation that it just feels like a money-grab. It's priced out a lot of long-term fans."In 2019, tickets ranged from £55 to £125. According to Ticket-Compare,, external UK inflation has since risen by about 32.4% and the cheapest NFL London tickets have risen by 43.9%. The most expensive have seen a 96.5% hike.Season-ticket packages had been available, guaranteeing seats for each London game with a discount, but they were scrapped after the 2024 season."It felt like a kick to the head for a lot of loyal fans who'd supported the games for a long time and spent a lot of money," said Cullen, a former season-ticket holder. "But I do understand the NFL wants to bring new fans in."Why NFL expansion is a 'double-edged sword'UK fans have also complained about the quality of recent match-ups in London when compared to those in the new countries where the NFL has expanded.Australia hosted a divisional clash between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams last month, while the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys played out a thriller in Brazil last week."It was an amazing game and we haven't had many of those unfortunately," added Cullen.The best team coming to London this year is Philadelphia, who have reached two of the past four Super Bowls, and their game next week is a sell-out even though it was the most expensive.The Jaguars face the Houston Texans in two weeks and Dave, another former season-ticket holder, will travel from Chorley."We were all gutted when they took the season tickets away," he admitted. "The way we saw it, we weren't wanted anymore because we didn't spend the money that new fans do on merchandise and we get to the stadium later."But it has opened it up for more fans to have the opportunity to attend so it's a double-edged sword."'One of the greatest events for neutrals'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jonathan Taylor ran in two touchdowns as the Colts beat the Commanders and produced a tea-sipping celebrationBBC Sport spoke to dozens of fans at Sunday's game and none of them were aware ticket prices had dropped. None seemed to care either.American fans know the London games don't provide the same tailgating experience they get back home, but they - and the players - are still fascinated by the eclectic crowd at international games.Fans still travel from all over the UK, Europe and the US, wearing jerseys of all the NFL teams."It's still one of the greatest sporting events that neutrals can go to," said Dave. "I don't think there's any other sport where you'd get tens of thousands watching teams they don't support."It was always a celebration of the game. People would go for the love of the sport rather than the two teams that were playing and I think that's still the same."It sure felt like a Washington home game when they recovered a Colts fumble on just the game's second play.The crowd produced an even bigger roar when third-choice quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis - replacing the injured Marcus Mariota - made a 47-yard touchdown pass to Treylon Burks in the third quarter.The Commanders thought they had drawn level when Antonio Williams ran in an 87-yard score, but the touchdown was chalked off for a Washington penalty.Indianapolis quarterback Daniel Jones then got in to seal their success, with Jonathan Taylor having run in two touchdowns for the Colts.Biles sprinkles stardust on London openerImage source, NFL/APImage caption, Simone Biles wore a customised outfit bearing her husband's name and numberIt is hard to imagine anyone went home disappointed, no matter what price they paid.The stands were bathed in sunshine and fans looked like they were having the time of their life as they sang Sweet Caroline and Wonderwall in unison.Oasis' Noel Gallagher was booed when he appeared on the big screen - no doubt because of his football allegiance to Manchester City - and former Manchester United and England striker Wayne Rooney was also among the crowd, wearing a half-and-half scarf.Olympian Simone Biles travelled to London to support her husband Jonathan Owens, who is a safety for the Colts, and as long as stars such as those show up at NFL games, international fans will want to be there too."There's been a lot of anger from fans on social media about the ticket prices but it's only what they do with last-minute holidays," added Dave."Even though some of us fans see it as poor way for the NFL to run it, they've got a full stadium."We're just not used to dynamic pricing in the UK. It was the same with Oasis tickets for their reunion. We were outraged at that but we still all went didn't we."

schema.headline: NFL London: 'Money-grab' or celebration? London series begins amid anger over ticket prices

title: Why Canada is wargaming a (long shot) US invasion
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.Noting the risk was low and the lik
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency."That's just risk management," Carney said.Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims."President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions."I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum."Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared."That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way."It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.So what would it be like if it happened?The first phase of a war could be quite short.According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a weekIts military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt."I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said."They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation."You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

schema.headline: Why Canada is wargaming a (long shot) US invasion

title: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you, from Jerry Hall and Richard E Grant to Rob and Romesh
description: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/BBC Creative/PA WireByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from
body: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/BBC Creative/PA WireByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first two episodes of The Celebrity Traitors"I know Rob very, very well. I mean, I've sat next to him as he's had a colonic."That was Romesh Ranganathan, reminding us - in case we were in any doubt - of his close friendship with Rob Beckett in the opening episode of The Celebrity Traitors.His words sum up the key difference between this series and the regular civilian version. In Celebrity Traitors, the players aren't just on-screen competitors - many actually know each other outside the show.Lots have worked together, and some are even friends. And those previous connections can have a huge impact on the show's dynamics.It's also partly why it is quite so delightful to watch - as friendships unravel, and former co-stars turn on each other.We've been unpicking the six degrees of separation. Here are some of the connections we've found - if you spot any more, we'd love to know. Get in touch with your thoughts in the comments section below.The Rob and Romesh bromanceThe dynamic between Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan is one of the most enjoyable to watch play out this year.As well as being great friends in real life, they have also worked together repeatedly, including in their travel show, Rob & Romesh Vs.They've also frequently made joint appearances on panel shows such as Mock the Week.But their friendship could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said ahead of the show.Image source, Joe Maher/Getty ImagesJoe and James are also friends (for now)Joe Lycett has said publicly that he's friends with James Acaster, and the pair have a running joke about how everyone gets them confused.They’ve also worked together on the TV show Travel Man.Lycett is also friends with Joanne McNally, external - he's described her as "one of my favourite people in the world".But those loyalties could be about to be tested, especially now that Acaster has been recruited as a traitor (anyone remember how things panned out for "good friends" Alan Carr and Paloma Faith...?)Lots of them are on the comedy circuitThere are SO many comedians in this year's series.And they are all likely to know each other. In addition to the alliances above, Joe Lycett was on the TV show Last One Laughing with Rob Beckett.Joanne McNally and Romesh Ranganathan appeared on game show Unacceptable together, and James Acaster went on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast.Speaking ahead of the show, McNally insisted she and her fellow comedians "haven't been in cahoots at all"."We know that we're more than willing to throw each other under the bus," she said.As for Acaster, he's admitted the other comedians are his “biggest threat” when it comes to being detected as a traitor.“Romesh, Joe, Rob know me really well. They all know that I don’t change my mind overnight,” he said, as he pondered whether to turn and help fellow traitor Richard E Grant clear his name.Maya has rubbed shoulders with several of the starsIt won’t surprise you that the two broadcasters of the group - Maya Jama and Amol Rajan - have met their fair share of the other stars before.Rajan had previously hosted both Michael Sheen and Joe Lycett on the Radio 2 Breakfast show, and also interviewed Romesh Ranganathan on BBC Asian Network.He's also been joined on the One Show on separate occasions by Ross Kemp, Miranda Hart and James Blunt - and earlier this year, he discussed AI on stage with Hannah Fry.But in the end, Rajan became the first player to be murdered, before we really got to see the impact of those past connections.Image source, Daniele Venturelli/WireImageImage caption, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Maya Jama were pictured together on the front row during Milan Fashion Week in 2024Meanwhile, Maya Jama is best known for hosting Love Island, but she's also popped up in loads of other places - including at this year's Brit Awards, where she presented an award with James Blunt.She's also been on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast, attended Milan Fashion Week with Leigh-Anne Pinnock, and she, Joe Lycett and James Acaster all appeared on The Big Fat Quiz of the Year.But Jama played down her connections on Celebrity Traitors, saying ahead of the show: “I've met a few people in the cast, but nobody really knows me, so we're all starting from scratch.”Bella and Sebastian are Westeros alumniUsually the younger celebs in the castle tend to know fewer people, but Bella Ramsey is pretty well connected.Notably, Ramsey and another younger cast member, Sebastian Croft, both starred in season six of Game of Thrones.Ramsey also worked with James Blunt on the film Sunny Dancer, was interviewed by James Acaster on his Off Menu podcast - and had a funny chat about their "vegan-ish" diet with Romesh Ranganathan on The Jonathan Ross Show.Ahead of the show, Croft said he didn't know many people aside from Ramsey before joining."One of the other things I'm excited about is this will be the first time I'm playing with people who, on the whole, don't know me and don't know how I work,” he said.Richard and Jerry go way back“I just don't believe Richard's a traitor. I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour.”That was American model Jerry Hall, speaking after actor Richard E Grant came under (admittedly self-inflicted) pressure in the opening episode of the series.As well as being neighbours, the pair are linked in lots of other ways.Image source, Rune Hellestad/Corbis via Getty ImagesImage caption, The pair pictured together at the Chelsea Flower Show in 2003Grant was pictured leaving Hall's wedding to Rupert Murdoch in 2016; in 2003, they were pictured together at Chelsea Flower Show, and they also acted in children's film Tooth back in 2004."It was ridiculous,"Jerry said of the film. "We had such a laugh, and I went on holiday with him earlier this year, just after Christmas to Africa with some friends. And we danced all night. We had so much fun! Little did we know back then that we'd both be here [on Celebrity Traitors]."Now they've taken the next step and moved in together, will they be arguing over who takes the bins out? We are here for it.Romesh and Julie are connected by The Weakest LinkYes, you know Romesh Ranganathan is the host of The Weakest Link.But did you know actor Julie Hesmondhalgh is the voiceover narrator for the quiz show?Here are a few other connections you may not have known about.Hesmondhalgh and Michael Sheen both fronted Papyrus's online child safety campaign back in 2020.YouTuber King Kenny was one of 10 online stars competing in the game show Would You Rather, hosted by Romesh Ranganathan.And singers James Blunt and Leigh-Anne Pinnock are both Brit Award winners. Both being successful musicians, it wouldn't be surprising if they have mingled together at events over the years.Where does this leave those with fewer friends?While some of the celebrities have known each other for 30 years, others have no friends in the castle at all.My Mad Fat Diary actor Sharon Rooney and Industry star Myha'la, for instance, have fewer connections than the others.And that can be a disadvantage. Remember Niko Omilana and Ruth Codd last year?After they were banished early on, a theory spread on social media that they were voted out because the other celebrities didn't know them that well.But it can definitely go both ways.Leigh-Anne Pinnock has said the fact she doesn't know many people might actually help her."I think I'm at a slight advantage because people just know me as Leigh-Anne from Little Mix, and they don't really know my personality that well," she said.What's clear is that these prior connections are "exactly the sort of thing" that makes Celebrity Traitors so fascinating, as TV reporter Siobhan Synnot told me.But - like Pinnock - she agrees that having loads of friends doesn't necessarily end up helping you."Quite often in The Traitors," she says, "that familiarity becomes a disadvantage".Players, you have been warned.When is The Celebrity Traitors next on TV?There are new episodes of The Celebrity Traitors every Thursday and Friday. The next episode is this Thursday 8 October at 8pm on BBC One and iPlayer, with another at the same time on Friday 9 October.The Celebrity Traitors: Uncloaked is next on this Thursday 8 October at 9.05pm on BBC One and iPlayer.

schema.headline: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you, from Jerry Hall and Richard E Grant to Rob and Romesh

title: Girl, 12, fatally shot in US during 'dispute over parking space'
description: A 12-year-old girl was killed in Baltimore over the weekend during an apparent disagreement over a parking space, police in the US city said. The girl
body: A 12-year-old girl was killed in Baltimore over the weekend during an apparent disagreement over a parking space, police in the US city said. The girl was caught in the crossfire of bullets between two men who police said were allegedly fighting over a parking space in a park where children were playing American football.In addition to the young girl, a woman was also found with gunshot wounds when police arrived on the scene. Two men also visited area hospitals for injuries believed to be related to the shooting, police said.Police are now searching for at least two suspects, Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said at a news conference. No arrests have been made."What we know is there was some type of argument between two cowards," Worley said. "They both opened fire on each other. In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl, who was probably down there watching football, was shot and killed."Worley said the girl, who police have not named, was not a target of the shooting.The girl was pronounced dead in hospital. The other three individuals who were injured have non-life-threatening injuries, Worley said.The incident happened after 18:00 EDT (23:00 BST) on Saturday.Authorities are still investigating the shooting and have asked any witnesses to bring information to police. It remains unclear how many shots were fired, Worley said. "Two grown men got into an argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone," Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said at the news conference. "We never should have to say something like that. What happened out here today is one of the most disgusting things I've ever seen in my life."

schema.headline: Girl, 12, fatally shot in US during 'dispute over parking space'

title: Daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians still at risk
description: The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.The safety of politi
body: The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years since the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe in July this year, Sir David's murder in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox's murder in 2016.The five years since her father was killed have been "absolutely devastating and heartbreaking", his daughter told Kuenssberg, adding: "It's a very, very real situation that we're living with."She has previously called for a public inquiry into the safety of politicians so people can have "the full facts to hand, full openness, honesty, and transparency".The nearing anniversary of Sir David's murder comes after the man accused of murdering Widdecombe was also charged with preparing acts of terror, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Amess, who knew Widdecombe as a family friend and called her Aunt Ann, said: "It's absolutely so tragic and heartbreaking that now she isn't here either." She added: "My dad was murdered five years ago so if so much has changed why are we still seeing other members of parliament or former members of parliament being targeted like this."Widdecombe was not a sitting member of parliament when she died, but was a member of the Conservative Party and the member for Maidstone and the Weald from 1987 to 2010. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29."I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this,"  she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be"."We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

schema.headline: Daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians still at risk

title: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says
description: US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on
body: US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995. She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days."He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors.He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said.Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday."If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be."He called on the governor to commute her death sentence to a life sentence "at the very least". "She has endured a torturous attempt at executing her," he said. "She's spent over 30 years in prison, most of that in solitary confinement.""We don't know right now - and we may never know - what sort of torture she endured during [her failed execution]."Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.Slemmer's mother May Martinez travelled to Nashville for the execution, which moved ahead despite last-minute legal challenges. Martinez, who supported Pike's death sentence, told local news outlet WJXX that she "broke down in tears" after finding out it was not successful. "I think that the state owes me a big apology," she said.The state's Department of Correction has defended the use of lethal injections, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.

schema.headline: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says

title: Protesters gather as migrants brought ashore at Gosport
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Police and demonstrators during the protest in Gosport on Sunday eveningUpdated 1 hour agoProtesters have gathere
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Police and demonstrators during the protest in Gosport on Sunday eveningUpdated 1 hour agoProtesters have gathered in a south coast town as more than 100 people believed to be migrants were brought ashore after crossing the Channel in a small boat.A number of people were seen arriving at a marina in Gosport, Hampshire, having been transported aboard two RNLI boats late on Sunday. Their dinghy appeared to have set off from near Utah Beach in Normandy during the morning, according to ship tracking data.French media reported there were about 120 migrants on board.Hampshire Police said it deployed officers to "support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea". The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act as well as powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The migrants were brought into Gosport onboard an RNLI boatA Home Office spokesperson said: "The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border."They added it was "vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival".A police cordon has been put in place on Haslar Road in Gosport, where the atmosphere at the protest mostly remained peaceful. Ambulances and coaches were also reportedly in the area.Some protesters stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Protesters gathered in Gosport on Sunday eveningThere were similar scenes last month when protesters gathered in the area expecting migrants to arrive on a dinghy, but they were ultimately taken to Dover by sea.Departures so far west along the south coast have been rare in recent years but it is the third such crossing in the space of a month.The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451.This is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

schema.headline: Protesters gather as migrants brought ashore at Gosport
